questionText: What is the Open/Closed Principle (OCP)?
option1: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules
option2: A class should have only one reason to change
option3: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types
option4: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification
correctOptionExplanation: OCP states that you should be able to add new behavior to a system (extension) without changing existing, already-tested code (modification).

questionText: Which SOLID letter does OCP represent?
option1: S
option2: I
option3: L
option4: O
correctOptionExplanation: OCP is the 'O' in SOLID.

questionText: Who is generally credited with originally coining the Open/Closed Principle?
option1: Bertrand Meyer
option2: Martin Fowler
option3: James Gosling
option4: Robert C. Martin
correctOptionExplanation: Bertrand Meyer introduced the Open/Closed concept; Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob) later popularized it as part of SOLID.

questionText: What does 'open for extension' mean under OCP?
option1: New behavior/functionality can be added to the system
option2: Any developer can modify any file freely
option3: Classes must always be marked open in Kotlin-style syntax
option4: Every class must be declared public
correctOptionExplanation: 'Open for extension' means the design allows new functionality to be added, typically through new classes implementing a shared abstraction.

questionText: What does 'closed for modification' mean under OCP?
option1: The class must be marked final
option2: Existing, already-tested code shouldn't need to be edited to support new functionality
option3: The class has no public methods
option4: The class cannot be extended by any subclass
correctOptionExplanation: 'Closed for modification' means the stable, verified source code of existing classes stays untouched when new behavior is introduced.

questionText: From the course notes, how is 'extension' under OCP typically achieved in Java, and what is explicitly NOT the way to extend?
option1: Achieved via inheritance/polymorphism; modification of the original class is explicitly not the way
option2: Achieved via making all methods static
option3: Achieved via modifying the original class directly; inheritance is not used
option4: Achieved via deleting the original class
correctOptionExplanation: The class notes explicitly frame OCP as: extend via inheritance, not via modifying the existing class.

questionText: In the IDiscount example (MembershipDiscount, CreditCardDiscount), what best demonstrates OCP?
option1: Adding a new CouponDiscount class implementing IDiscount without changing any existing discount classes or the code that uses IDiscount
option2: Adding an if-else check for coupon logic inside MembershipDiscount
option3: Deleting CreditCardDiscount to make room for CouponDiscount
option4: Renaming IDiscount every time a new discount type is added
correctOptionExplanation: OCP is demonstrated when a brand-new discount type can be added purely by creating a new class implementing the existing interface, with zero changes to existing code.

questionText: In the DogSoundManager.makeSound(IDog dog) example, how would you add a new Beagle breed in an OCP-compliant way?
option1: Add a new overloaded makeSound(Beagle dog) method
option2: Edit makeSound() to add an if (dog instanceof Beagle) branch
option3: Change IDog into a concrete class first
option4: Create a new Beagle class implementing IDog; DogSoundManager itself requires no changes
correctOptionExplanation: Because makeSound() already depends on the IDog abstraction, any new implementing class like Beagle can be plugged in without touching DogSoundManager.

questionText: What's a classic anti-pattern that violates OCP?
option1: A class with a private constructor
option2: A method with no parameters
option3: A class implementing a single interface
option4: A long if-else or switch statement that branches on a type, requiring edits every time a new type is added
correctOptionExplanation: Conditional type-checking logic (if/switch on type) that must be edited for every new case is the textbook OCP violation.

questionText: Given `if (type.equals("CREDIT")) {...} else if (type.equals("COUPON")) {...}` inside a PaymentProcessor, why does this violate OCP?
option1: It violates the Liskov Substitution Principle instead
option2: Adding a new payment type requires modifying this existing, already-tested method
option3: It uses interfaces incorrectly
option4: It has too many private fields
correctOptionExplanation: Every new payment type forces an edit to this method, which is exactly the modification OCP tries to prevent.

questionText: What is the OCP-compliant fix for the PaymentProcessor if/else example?
option1: Add more else-if branches as new payment types arrive
option2: Convert the method to a static utility method
option3: Hardcode all payment types into an enum with no interface
option4: Define a Payment interface implemented by CreditPayment, CouponPayment, etc., and call payment.process() polymorphically
correctOptionExplanation: Replacing type-checking branches with polymorphism lets you add new payment types as new classes, without editing the processing logic.

questionText: What is the core mechanism in Java that makes OCP-compliant designs possible?
option1: The final keyword
option2: Primitive data types
option3: Polymorphism, via interfaces or abstract classes
option4: Static methods
correctOptionExplanation: Polymorphism lets calling code depend on a stable abstraction while new concrete implementations provide new behavior — the technical foundation of OCP.

questionText: What role do interfaces/abstract classes play in supporting OCP?
option1: They must always be modified whenever new behavior is added
option2: They are unrelated to OCP
option3: They define the stable, 'closed' contract that consuming code depends on, while new concrete classes provide the 'open' extension point
option4: They prevent any class from ever being extended
correctOptionExplanation: The interface/abstract class stays fixed (closed), while new implementing classes deliver new behavior (open for extension).

questionText: What real benefit does OCP provide regarding regression risk?
option1: Adding new functionality via new classes is unlikely to break already-tested existing code, since that code isn't touched
option2: OCP guarantees there will never be any bugs
option3: OCP has no effect on regression risk
option4: OCP eliminates the need for any tests on new code
correctOptionExplanation: Because existing, verified code paths remain unmodified, the risk of introducing regressions when adding new features is significantly reduced.

questionText: What real benefit does OCP provide for team collaboration on new features?
option1: It has no effect on collaboration
option2: Multiple developers can add new implementations (e.g., new discount types) simultaneously without editing a shared class, avoiding merge conflicts
option3: It prevents developers from writing new classes
option4: It requires only one developer to ever add new features
correctOptionExplanation: Because extension happens via new classes rather than edits to shared code, concurrent feature work is less likely to collide.

questionText: What real benefit does OCP provide for evolving business requirements over time?
option1: It requires rewriting the entire system for every new rule
option2: It prevents the business from ever changing its requirements
option3: New business rules (like new discount policies) can be handled by adding new code rather than editing stable, already-verified logic
option4: It only works for read-only systems
correctOptionExplanation: OCP-friendly systems accommodate new requirements as additive changes, keeping the core, proven logic untouched and safe.

questionText: Does OCP mean you should never modify any existing code, ever?
option1: Yes, absolutely no code can ever be changed once written
option2: Yes, but only test code can be modified
option3: No, it means well-designed abstractions shouldn't require modification for anticipated kinds of extension; the abstraction itself may still occasionally evolve
option4: No, OCP only applies to private methods
correctOptionExplanation: OCP is a design goal for anticipated extension points, not an absolute ban on ever touching code; abstractions can still evolve when genuinely necessary.

questionText: What is a potential downside of over-applying OCP?
option1: There are no downsides to applying OCP anywhere
option2: OCP always makes code run faster with zero downsides
option3: OCP eliminates the need for interfaces entirely
option4: Premature or speculative abstraction can add unnecessary complexity if the guessed extension points are never actually used
correctOptionExplanation: Introducing abstraction for extension points that never materialize can add indirection and complexity without real benefit — a common critique of over-engineering.

questionText: What is the Strategy design pattern, and how does it relate to OCP?
option1: It encapsulates interchangeable algorithms/behaviors behind a common interface, letting new strategies be added without modifying existing code — a classic way to implement OCP
option2: It has no relationship to OCP
option3: It's a pattern for managing database transactions only
option4: It requires all strategies to be static methods
correctOptionExplanation: The Strategy pattern is one of the most direct implementations of OCP: new behavior variants are added as new classes implementing a shared interface.

questionText: Is the IDiscount setup (MembershipDiscount, CreditCardDiscount, CouponDiscount) an example of the Strategy Pattern?
option1: No, it's an example of the Singleton pattern
option2: Yes, each discount type is an interchangeable strategy implementing the shared IDiscount interface
option3: No, it's an example of the Observer pattern
option4: No, Strategy pattern requires abstract classes only
correctOptionExplanation: Multiple interchangeable implementations behind one interface, selected/swapped by the client, is precisely the Strategy pattern in action.

questionText: Given `IDiscount ds = new MembershipDiscount();`, what should you do to add CreditCardDiscount support while staying OCP-compliant?
option1: Change ds's declared type to MembershipDiscount specifically
option2: Add an if-else inside MembershipDiscount to also handle credit card logic
option3: Delete IDiscount and hardcode logic directly
option4: Create a new class implementing IDiscount, without modifying existing discount classes or the code that consumes IDiscount
correctOptionExplanation: OCP-compliant extension means adding a new implementing class, leaving existing classes and consuming code unchanged.

questionText: When adding CouponDiscount to an existing OCP-compliant discount system, which existing classes need modification?
option1: MembershipDiscount and CreditCardDiscount must both be edited
option2: All classes in the entire codebase must be recompiled and changed
option3: None — only a new CouponDiscount class needs to be added
option4: The IDiscount interface must be deleted and rewritten
correctOptionExplanation: A properly abstracted, OCP-compliant system lets you add new discount types purely additively, with zero edits to existing classes.

questionText: What's the danger of instead adding a new `if (discountType == COUPON)` branch inside an existing shared method to support coupons?
option1: It automatically improves performance
option2: It only affects the CouponDiscount class
option3: It violates OCP, risks breaking existing discount logic, and forces re-testing of the entire modified method
option4: It has no downsides and is the recommended approach
correctOptionExplanation: Editing a shared method to add new type-specific logic is a direct OCP violation, introducing regression risk to previously working, tested behavior.

questionText: Does OCP apply only to classes, or also to functions and modules?
option1: It applies only to private methods
option2: It applies broadly to any software entity — functions, classes, modules, and beyond
option3: It applies only to interfaces, never classes
option4: It applies strictly only to classes named 'Manager'
correctOptionExplanation: The Open/Closed idea generalizes to any unit of software design where new behavior might need to be added over time.

questionText: How does OCP help reduce the 'blast radius' of adding a new feature in a large codebase?
option1: It only helps for codebases smaller than 100 lines
option2: New features are added as new code, so the probability of unintentionally affecting unrelated existing behavior drops significantly
option3: It has no effect on blast radius at all
option4: It guarantees the entire codebase must be redeployed for every change
correctOptionExplanation: Because extension happens additively rather than through edits to shared logic, the scope of what could be affected by a new feature stays narrow.

questionText: What design pattern lets subclasses override specific steps of a fixed algorithm structure, embodying OCP through abstract classes?
option1: Adapter Pattern
option2: Builder Pattern
option3: Singleton Pattern
option4: Template Method Pattern
correctOptionExplanation: The Template Method pattern defines a fixed algorithm skeleton in a base class (closed) while letting subclasses override specific steps (open for extension).

questionText: What is a common code smell signaling an OCP violation across a codebase?
option1: A class with a single well-defined interface
option2: Use of the final keyword on a class
option3: Consistent naming conventions across classes
option4: Repeated instanceof/type-checking or switch-on-type logic scattered across multiple methods to decide behavior
correctOptionExplanation: Scattered type-checks that must all be updated for every new type are a strong signal that polymorphism should replace them for OCP compliance.

questionText: Why is scattering type-checks across multiple methods worse than a clean, OCP-compliant design?
option1: It has no real downside compared to polymorphism
option2: It always runs faster than polymorphic dispatch
option3: It automatically documents itself
option4: Every new type requires hunting down and editing every scattered check, increasing the chance of missing one and introducing bugs
correctOptionExplanation: Centralizing behavior differences behind polymorphism (OCP) avoids the maintenance burden and error-risk of hunting down every scattered conditional.

questionText: Does adding a brand-new required method to an existing interface (like IDiscount) count as respecting OCP for classes that already implement it?
option1: No, it actually breaks OCP for existing implementers, since they'd fail to compile until updated with the new method
option2: Yes, because interfaces can never be modified anyway
option3: Yes, existing implementers are automatically unaffected
option4: No, but only if the interface is marked final
correctOptionExplanation: Changing an existing interface's contract forces every current implementer to be edited, which is itself a modification-driven change — a known tension in evolving interfaces under OCP.

questionText: How can you add new behavior to an interface without breaking OCP for existing implementers (Java 8+)?
option1: Convert the interface into an abstract class first
option2: Add the new behavior as a default method with a sensible default implementation
option3: Mark the new method as private
option4: Force every implementing class to be rewritten immediately
correctOptionExplanation: Default methods let you evolve an interface with new capabilities while existing implementations continue compiling unchanged, preserving OCP for them.

questionText: Why are OCP-friendly systems often described as more resilient to changing business requirements?
option1: Because they eliminate the need for requirements gathering
option2: Because new requirements can typically be met by adding new implementations rather than rewriting core, stable logic
option3: Because they only work for static, unchanging businesses
option4: Because they require no further development ever
correctOptionExplanation: Systems built around stable abstractions can absorb new business rules as additive extensions, without destabilizing the tested core.

questionText: Does OCP eliminate the need to test newly added code (like a new subclass)?
option1: No, new extensions still need their own tests; OCP just protects already-tested existing code from being disturbed
option2: Yes, but only if the new class is private
option3: Yes, new code never needs testing once OCP is applied
option4: No, but only integration tests are needed, never unit tests
correctOptionExplanation: OCP reduces risk to existing code, but any new class/behavior still requires its own verification through testing.

questionText: If a class's core logic must be edited every time a new business rule or type is introduced, which SOLID principle is most likely being violated?
option1: Open/Closed Principle
option2: None, this is completely normal and expected
option3: Interface Segregation Principle only
option4: Dependency Injection exclusively
correctOptionExplanation: Needing to repeatedly modify existing core logic for every new rule/type is the hallmark symptom of an OCP violation.

questionText: Why is OCP especially valuable in regulated or mission-critical software?
option1: Because OCP is a legal requirement in all industries
option2: Because it removes the need for audits entirely
option3: Because untouched, already-verified/certified code doesn't need to be re-tested or re-certified just because new features were added elsewhere
option4: Because regulated software never needs any testing
correctOptionExplanation: In high-stakes domains, avoiding modification to already-certified code paths when adding features can meaningfully reduce costly re-verification and re-certification work.

questionText: What's a practical tip for spotting good OCP extension points in existing code?
option1: Look for any class that has a constructor
option2: Look for classes with the fewest lines of code
option3: Look for places with 'if type == X' branches (or likely to grow that way) and consider replacing them with an interface plus polymorphism
option4: Look for the longest method in the codebase and leave it untouched
correctOptionExplanation: Type-branching conditionals that are likely to grow are prime candidates for refactoring into polymorphic, OCP-compliant designs.

questionText: Which best summarizes the primary real-world benefit of applying OCP consistently?
option1: It guarantees the codebase never needs any new classes again
option2: It only benefits small codebases under 500 lines
option3: Systems can grow with new features safely by adding new code rather than editing stable, tested code, minimizing regression risk and enabling faster, more confident delivery
option4: It eliminates the need for a QA/testing process entirely
correctOptionExplanation: OCP's central payoff is safer, faster growth: new capability is layered on top of proven, untouched foundations instead of risking destabilizing them.

questionText: From the course notes, OCP was summarized with the phrase 'class -> extension -> inheritance, X modification.' What does the crossed-out 'modification' signify?
option1: Modification is the preferred way to add new behavior
option2: Modification of existing classes is explicitly the thing OCP wants you to avoid when adding new behavior
option3: Modification refers to changing method names only
option4: It has no particular meaning in the notes
correctOptionExplanation: The notes explicitly frame extension via inheritance as correct and modifying the existing class as the thing to avoid, matching OCP's definition.

questionText: Which of these two designs is more OCP-compliant for a notification system supporting Email, SMS, and (soon) Push notifications?
option1: A single sendNotification(String type) method with an if-else per notification type
option2: Hardcoding email-sending logic directly inside every class that needs to notify someone
option3: A single class with one huge method containing all notification logic inline
option4: A Notifier interface implemented by EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier, and later PushNotifier, called polymorphically
correctOptionExplanation: An interface-based design lets you add PushNotifier later without touching existing EmailNotifier/SmsNotifier code or the calling logic — the OCP-compliant approach.

questionText: In the Notifier example, what happens to existing EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier code when PushNotifier is added?
option1: They must be deleted and replaced
option2: They must be merged into a single class with PushNotifier
option3: Nothing — they remain unmodified since PushNotifier is simply a new class implementing the same interface
option4: They must both be rewritten to accommodate PushNotifier
correctOptionExplanation: This is the practical payoff of OCP: existing implementations stay completely untouched when a new one is added.

questionText: Why is polymorphism described as 'the technical foundation' for OCP rather than inheritance alone?
option1: Because inheritance alone always violates OCP
option2: Because it's the ability to call the correct new implementation through a shared abstraction at runtime that lets new classes plug in without changing calling code
option3: Because polymorphism only works with abstract classes, never interfaces
option4: Because polymorphism and OCP are entirely unrelated concepts
correctOptionExplanation: While inheritance/interface implementation establishes the relationship, it's polymorphic dispatch at runtime that actually lets new implementations be substituted transparently for OCP to work in practice.

questionText: What's the relationship between OCP and the Dependency Inversion Principle (the 'D' in SOLID)?
option1: OCP requires violating DIP to work correctly
option2: Both rely on depending on abstractions rather than concrete implementations, letting new concrete classes be swapped in without changing high-level code
option3: DIP is only about database connections
option4: They are unrelated principles with nothing in common
correctOptionExplanation: OCP and DIP are closely linked: depending on stable abstractions (DIP) is what makes it possible to extend behavior via new implementations without modification (OCP).

questionText: A ReportExporter class has a method exportReport(String format) with if/else branches for PDF, CSV, and Excel. What's the OCP concern here?
option1: It's fine because it uses a String parameter
option2: This only concerns the Single Responsibility Principle, not OCP
option3: There is no OCP concern since export logic naturally belongs together
option4: Adding a new export format (e.g., JSON) requires modifying this existing, already-tested method
correctOptionExplanation: Every new format requires editing shared logic, which is exactly the kind of modification OCP aims to prevent as the system grows.

questionText: What's the OCP-compliant fix for the ReportExporter example?
option1: Remove support for CSV and Excel entirely
option2: Add a new else-if branch every time a format is added, forever
option3: Define an Exporter interface implemented by PdfExporter, CsvExporter, ExcelExporter, etc., selected and called polymorphically
option4: Merge all export logic into one giant method for 'simplicity'
correctOptionExplanation: An interface-based exporter design lets you add new formats as new classes without touching the existing, tested exporters or the calling code.

questionText: Does following OCP typically increase or decrease the total number of classes in a codebase compared to a single, type-switching class?
option1: It typically increases the number of classes, trading a bit of upfront structure for long-term safer extensibility
option2: It has no effect on the number of classes ever
option3: It only applies if there's exactly one class in the project
option4: It always decreases the number of classes to just one
correctOptionExplanation: OCP-compliant designs favor several small, focused implementation classes over one large branching class, which is a deliberate trade-off for safer future extension.

questionText: Why is 'closed for modification' particularly important for code that's already in production and heavily relied upon?
option1: Because modifying well-tested, production-proven code risks introducing new bugs into behavior that many parts of the system already depend on
option2: Because modification is always faster than extension
option3: Because production code is automatically bug-free
option4: Because production code can never be read again
correctOptionExplanation: Code already running in production has accumulated implicit trust and test coverage; touching it to add unrelated new behavior risks destabilizing what already works.

questionText: A class calculates shipping cost using `if (region == "US") {...} else if (region == "EU") {...}`. Which principle is most directly violated as more regions get added?
option1: Liskov Substitution Principle
option2: Open/Closed Principle
option3: Single Responsibility Principle only
option4: Interface Segregation Principle
correctOptionExplanation: Needing to keep editing this method every time a new region is introduced is a direct OCP violation, best solved with a ShippingStrategy interface per region.

questionText: What would an OCP-compliant redesign of the shipping cost example look like?
option1: A single hardcoded shipping cost for every region
option2: Removing shipping cost calculation entirely
option3: One method with an ever-growing list of else-if branches, accepted as unavoidable
option4: A ShippingCostStrategy interface with one implementation class per region (USShipping, EUShipping, etc.), selected and invoked polymorphically
correctOptionExplanation: Encapsulating each region's shipping rule behind a shared interface lets new regions be added as new classes without editing the existing calculation logic.

questionText: Can OCP be violated even in a system that uses interfaces, if the interface itself keeps changing to accommodate every new case?
option1: No, using any interface automatically guarantees full OCP compliance forever
option2: Yes, but only if the interface has more than 10 methods
option3: No, interfaces are immune to violating OCP by definition
option4: Yes, constantly redefining the interface's contract to fit new cases is itself a form of modification, undermining OCP's goal
correctOptionExplanation: Simply using an interface isn't enough; if its contract must be reworked for every new requirement, the design still suffers from the same modification risk OCP tries to avoid.

questionText: What's a good sign that a class or interface is genuinely OCP-compliant in practice?
option1: The class was written more than a year ago
option2: The class has never been tested even once
option3: New requirements can repeatedly be satisfied by adding new classes, while the original interface and existing implementations stay untouched over multiple change cycles
option4: The class has zero public methods
correctOptionExplanation: Real-world validation of OCP comes from observing, over time, that new features keep landing as new additive classes rather than edits to the stable core.

questionText: Overall, why is OCP considered one of the most impactful SOLID principles for long-lived software systems?
option1: Because it's the only principle that involves interfaces
option2: Because it's the easiest principle to apply and requires no design effort
option3: Because it eliminates the need for the other four SOLID principles
option4: Because most real systems must keep growing with new features, and OCP directly targets doing that safely without destabilizing what already works
correctOptionExplanation: Long-lived systems inevitably need new features; OCP directly addresses how to add them safely, making it especially valuable as software ages and grows.
